verdict.reasoning: Patient reports a really bad, throbbing headache for about a day, mainly on the left side, and notes it seems worse in light rooms or sunlight (“really bad headache… had it for about a day… mainly on the left side… quite sensitive to light… worse when I'm in a light room or like sunlight”).

Duration and character are confirmed (“really bad headache… had it for about a day… kind of throbbing… mainly on the left side”). Improvement lying down is stated (“I think I've generally been lying down. Seems to be better that way”). Worsening in bright light is stated (“worse when I'm in a light room or like sunlight”).

Onset on waking yesterday is confirmed (“since yesterday morning, since I woke up, really”). Fluctuation without full resolution is confirmed (“just kind of fade? So it's still there a little bit, but it kind of gets more or less severe”).

Patient denies visual symptoms and abnormal smells/tastes (“Any problems with your eyes or your eyesight? Patient: No, not at all… Any abnormal smells or tastes? Patient: No”). Aura is not explicitly asked but denial of visual and sensory phenomena is consistent with no aura being reported.
Patient denies nausea/vomiting and reports normal intake (“Any nausea, vomiting? Patient: No, no, I've been feeling fine… Have you been eating and drinking okay? Patient: Yes, yes, same as normal”).

She denies fever and URTI symptoms (“Have you had any other symptoms like feeling feverish, temperature, any runny nose, sore ears? Patient: No, not really. Any sort of cold symptoms? I was doing okay the day before”). She also denies cough (“Any problems if you cough or sneeze? Patient: No, but I haven't really got a cough or anything”).
Neurologic review is negative (“any problems with weakness, tingling, numbness in your arms or legs? Patient: No, not at all”).

New headache with no prior history is confirmed (“Normally, do you get any headaches? Patient: No, not really. It's not something I've ever had before… this headache is new to you and you've not had regular headaches before? Patient: Yeah”).
Menstrual timing and lack of association are stated (“has it occurred at a particular time in your menstrual cycle? Patient: No, not particularly. My period was about a week ago”).
Aspirin intolerance is documented (“I'm allergic to aspirin, so I haven't been taking that… What happens when you take aspirin? Patient: I just feel really sick”).
Current use of paracetamol is stated (“What tablets have you been taking already for it?… Patient: Just paracetamol”).

Microgynon use and duration are documented (“Do you take any medication? Patient: No, just contraception… Which contraception? Patient: Microgynon… When did you start that one? Patient: About six years ago”).
Reaction to aspirin is described as nausea (“I'm allergic to aspirin… What happens when you take aspirin? Patient: I just feel really sick”).
Family history of hypertension is recorded (“My mum had high blood pressure”).
Family history of migraines is recorded (“she's got a history of migraines”).
Living situation is described (“Who do you live with at home? Patient: Just with housemates, just friends”).
Alcohol intake is described as a few drinks at weekends (“Do you drink much alcohol day to day? Patient: I'd say a normal amount probably, you know, a few drinks at the weekend”).
Non-smoking status is explicit (“Do you smoke? Patient: No”).
Denial of other drug use is explicit (“Do you take any other drugs of any sort? Patient: No”).

The features are stated (acute unilateral throbbing headache with photophobia, new onset, no red flags). The GP’s impression is migraine (“it does sound quite like a migraine”). Safety-netting covers red flags, but none are elicited in the history.
Microgynon use is documented, but the clinician does not state that the combined pill is considered relevant to the headache history; no such link is discussed in the transcript.
The need for a blood pressure check is explicitly mentioned (“I would try and manage to get your blood pressure checked if you haven't had a chat for a while”).
Aspirin intolerance is acknowledged during assessment (“I'm allergic to aspirin… What happens when you take aspirin? I just feel really sick”).
Plan includes NSAID with paracetamol (“What I would suggest is taking some anti inflammatories along with a paracetamol”). Ibuprofen is given as an example earlier in discussion of NSAIDs.
Hydration advice is explicitly given (“Make sure you're really well hydrated and see how that goes”).
Rest in a dark and quiet room is not discussed; patient only mentions self-chosen behavior of staying in because light worsens headache, but this is not given as clinician advice.

Safety net advice is given: return if not settling or getting worse, any change in headache, high temperature, or rash (“if it isn't settling or it's getting worse or you get any other change in your headache or you're unwell with it with a high temperature, then we would certainly need to speak to you straight away… if you have a raised temperature or headaches just getting worse and we develop any rashes or anything like that, then we'd need to speak to you straight away”). New neurological deficits are not named but are reasonably encompassed by “any other change in your headache or you're unwell with it.”

Clinician advises arranging a BP check, which implies at a suitable location (“I would try and manage to get your blood pressure checked if you haven't had a chat for a while”). Pharmacy/clinic is not specified but planning a check is supported.
Advice to obtain a thermometer is explicit (“Another thing to do is to have a thermometer at home so you make sure that your temperature is okay”).

Follow-up for recurrent or cyclical headaches is advised (“if you're getting persistent headaches or headaches associated with your menstrual cycle or certain things seem to trigger these headaches, then it would be worth having a further discussion about it”).
